title: 1 Corinthians

stories.title: 📜 1 Corinthians 1
summaryBullets: Paul, called to be an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and our brother Sosthenes, (1:1).

To the church of God in Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus and called to be holy, together with all those everywhere who call on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, their Lord and ours: (1:2).
Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. (1:3).
I always thank my God for you because of the grace He has given you in Christ Jesus. (1:4).
For in Him you have been enriched in every way, in all speech and all knowledge, (1:5).
because our testimony about Christ was confirmed in you. (1:6).
Therefore you do not lack any spiritual gift as you eagerly await the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ. (1:7).
He will sustain you to the end, so that you will be blameless on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. (1:8).
God, who has called you into fellowship with His Son Jesus Christ our Lord, is faithful. (1:9).
I appeal to you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that all of you agree together, so that there may be no divisions among you and that you may be united in mind and conviction. (1:10).
My brothers, some from Chloe’s household have informed me that there are quarrels among you. (1:11).
What I mean is this: Individuals among you are saying, “I follow Paul,” “I follow Apollos,” “I follow Cephas,” or “I follow Christ.” (1:12).
Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Were you baptized into the name of Paul? (1:13).
I thank God that I did not baptize any of you except Crispus and Gaius, (1:14).
so no one can say that you were baptized into my name. (1:15).
Yes, I also baptized the household of Stephanas; beyond that I do not remember if I baptized anyone else. (1:16).
For Christ did not send me to baptize, but to preach the gospel, not with words of wisdom, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power. (1:17).
For the message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God. (1:18).
For it is written: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise; the intelligence of the intelligent I will frustrate.” (1:19).
Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the philosopher of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world? (1:20).
For since in the wisdom of God the world through its wisdom did not know Him, God was pleased through the foolishness of what was preached to save those who believe. (1:21).
Jews demand signs and Greeks search for wisdom, (1:22).
but we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles, (1:23).
but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God. (1:24).
For the foolishness of God is wiser than man’s wisdom, and the weakness of God is stronger than man’s strength. (1:25).
Brothers, consider the time of your calling: Not many of you were wise by human standards; not many were powerful; not many were of noble birth. (1:26).
But God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise; God chose the weak things of the world to shame the strong. (1:27).
He chose the lowly and despised things of the world, and the things that are not, to nullify the things that are, (1:28).
so that no one may boast in His presence. (1:29).
It is because of Him that you are in Christ Jesus, who has become for us wisdom from God: our righteousness, holiness, and redemption. (1:30).
Therefore, as it is written: “Let him who boasts boast in the Lord.” (1:31).
crossRefs: Romans 1:7: Called saints.
Philippians 1:6: He will complete the good work.
1 Thessalonians 5:24: Faithful is he who calls you.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קָדוֹשׁ (qādwōš), Greek: ἡγιασμένοι (ἡgiasmέnoi, NT), Aramaic: מקדש (מקדש)
translationNotes.note: Means set apart or made holy for God’s use.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֵדוּת (ʿēdwt, sense), Greek: μαρτύριον τοῦ Χριστοῦ (martύrion toῦ Christoῦ, NT), Aramaic: סהדותא דמשיחא (סהדותא דמשיחא)
translationNotes.note: Refers to the witness or confirmation of Christ’s message among them.

Originally professional copyists of Scripture. By the New Testament era, scholar-teachers of the Law; often, though not exclusively, aligned with the Pharisees. They formed the educated religious class that adjudicated everyday halakhic questions.
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סוֹפֵר (sopher); Greek: γραμματεύς (grammateus)
Greek: Κόρινθος (Korinthos)
translationNotes.note: Corinth sat on the four-mile neck of land joining southern Greece to the mainland, with a harbor on each side: Lechaeum facing west toward Italy and Cenchreae facing east toward Asia, which is where Phoebe's church was (Romans 16:1) and where Paul shaved his head (Acts 18:18). Rather than sail the long dangerous way round the Peloponnese, shippers hauled goods, and sometimes whole small ships, across the isthmus on a paved trackway. Rome destroyed the old Greek city in 146 BC; Julius Caesar refounded it as a Roman colony in 44 BC and settled it largely with freed slaves, and it became the capital of the province of Achaia. It was under a century old when Paul arrived.

translationNotes.original: Greek: εὐγενεῖς (eugeneis), well-born
translationNotes.note: Roman society was ranked and everyone knew where they stood: senators, then the equestrian order, then the town councillors of a colony, then freeborn citizens, then freedmen, then slaves. Paul's point in 1:26 is a head count of that ranking inside the church, and it is not a metaphor. The one Corinthian believer named with a public office is Erastus, the city treasurer of Romans 16:23; a paving stone dug up beside the theater at Corinth in 1929 carries an inscription reading that Erastus laid the pavement at his own expense in return for his aedileship.

translationNotes.term: Jews demand signs and Greeks search for wisdom
translationNotes.original: Greek: σοφία (sophia), wisdom - μωρία (moria), folly
translationNotes.note: Both halves of 1:22 name a real cultural appetite. Rhetoric and philosophy were the prestige pursuits of a Greek city; a man's standing rose with his ability to argue elegantly in public, and traveling speakers drew paying crowds. Against that, crucifixion was the death Rome kept for slaves and rebels, deliberately public and deliberately shameful, and no respectable Roman would have chosen it as the center of a message. That collision is what Paul calls folly to the Greeks and a stumbling block to the Jews.

stories.keyTakeaway: After thanksgiving Paul appeals for unity, since quarrels have divided the church into followings of Paul, Apollos, Cephas, and Christ; the message of the cross is foolishness to the perishing but the power of God to those being saved, for God chose the foolish and weak things of the world so that no one may boast except in the Lord.

stories.title: 📜 1 Corinthians 2
summaryBullets: When I came to you, brothers, I did not come with eloquence or wisdom as I proclaimed to you the testimony about God. (2:1).
For I resolved to know nothing while I was with you except Jesus Christ and Him crucified. (2:2).
I came to you in weakness and fear, and with much trembling. (2:3).
My message and my preaching were not with persuasive words of wisdom, but with a demonstration of the Spirit’s power, (2:4).
so that your faith would not rest on men’s wisdom, but on God’s power. (2:5).
Among the mature, however, we speak a message of wisdom — but not the wisdom of this age or of the rulers of this age, who are coming to nothing. (2:6).
No, we speak of the mysterious and hidden wisdom of God, which He destined for our glory before time began. (2:7).
None of the rulers of this age understood it. For if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. (2:8).
Rather, as it is written: “No eye has seen, no ear has heard, no heart has imagined, what God has prepared for those who love Him.” (2:9).
But God has revealed it to us by the Spirit. The Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God. (2:10).
For who among men knows the thoughts of man except his own spirit within him? So too, no one knows the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God. (2:11).
We have not received the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God, that we may understand what God has freely given us. (2:12).
And this is what we speak, not in words taught us by human wisdom, but in words taught by the Spirit, expressing spiritual truths in spiritual words. (2:13).
The natural man does not accept the things that come from the Spirit of God. For they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them, because they are spiritually discerned. (2:14).
The spiritual man judges all things, but he himself is not subject to anyone’s judgment. (2:15).
“For who has known the mind of the Lord, so as to instruct Him?” But we have the mind of Christ. (2:16).
crossRefs: Isaiah 64:4: No eye has seen a God besides you, who acts for the one who waits for him.
Isaiah 40:13: Who has directed the Spirit of the LORD, or as his counselor has instructed him?
Acts 18:1-11: Paul arrives in Corinth from Athens, works at his trade with Aquila, and stays a year and six months.
Daniel 2:20-23: God reveals deep and hidden things and gives wisdom to the wise.
Matthew 16:17: Flesh and blood did not reveal this to Peter, but the Father in heaven.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אִוֶּלֶת (ʾiwelet), Greek: μωρία (mōrίa, NT), Aramaic: סכלותא (סכלותא)
translationNotes.note: Denotes foolishness or absurdity; Paul applies it to how the cross appears to unbelievers.

translationNotes.original: Greek: ψυχικός (psychikos) - πνευματικός (pneumatikos)
translationNotes.note: The word rendered 'natural' in 2:14 is psychikos, built on psyche, the soul or life. It means soulish, a person running on nothing but ordinary human life, and it is set against pneumatikos, the one the Spirit has worked on. English 'natural' suggests a contrast with the supernatural; the Greek contrast is between two sources of life, and James 3:15 and Jude 1:19 use the same word.

translationNotes.original: Greek: Κόρινθος (Korinthos)
translationNotes.note: Paul reached Corinth from Athens with no money and no reputation, and worked at his trade while he taught (Acts 18:1-4), which is the weakness and trembling he mentions in 2:3. The visit can be dated: a stone at Delphi carrying a letter of the emperor Claudius names Gallio as proconsul of Achaia, which puts his year in office at AD 51 to 52, and Acts 18:12 has Paul hauled before that same Gallio.

translationNotes.original: Greek: μυστήριον (mysterion)
translationNotes.note: Not a puzzle to be worked out. A mysterion was what initiates in a Greek cult were shown and outsiders were not, and Paul uses the word for what God kept hidden and has now disclosed. He calls it hidden wisdom destined for our glory before time began at 2:7, and Colossians 1:26 gives the same shape: hidden for ages, now revealed to His saints.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul explains that he preached to the Corinthians not with eloquent words but with a demonstration of the Spirit's power, and that God's wisdom - hidden before time and rejected by the rulers of this age - is revealed to believers through the Spirit, not human understanding.

headings.text: Paul’s Message by the Spirit’s Power

stories.title: 📜 1 Corinthians 3
summaryBullets: Brothers, I could not address you as spiritual, but as worldly — as infants in Christ. (3:1).
I gave you milk, not solid food, for you were not yet ready for solid food. In fact, you are still not ready, (3:2).
for you are still worldly. For since there is jealousy and dissension among you, are you not worldly? Are you not walking in the way of man? (3:3).
For when one of you says, “I follow Paul,” and another, “I follow Apollos,” are you not mere men? (3:4).
What then is Apollos? And what is Paul? They are servants through whom you believed, as the Lord has assigned to each his role. (3:5).
I planted the seed and Apollos watered it, but God made it grow. (3:6).
So neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but only God, who makes things grow. (3:7).
He who plants and he who waters are one in purpose, and each will be rewarded according to his own labor. (3:8).
For we are God’s fellow workers; you are God’s field, God’s building. (3:9).
By the grace God has given me, I laid a foundation as an expert builder, and someone else is building on it. But each one must be careful how he builds. (3:10).
For no one can lay a foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ. (3:11).
If anyone builds on this foundation using gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, or straw, (3:12).
his workmanship will be evident, because the Day will bring it to light. It will be revealed with fire, and the fire will prove the quality of each man’s work. (3:13).
If what he has built survives, he will receive a reward. (3:14).
If it is burned up, he will suffer loss. He himself will be saved, but only as if through the flames. (3:15).
Do you not know that you yourselves are God’s temple, and that God’s Spirit dwells in you? (3:16).
If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him; for God’s temple is holy, and you are that temple. (3:17).
Let no one deceive himself. If any of you thinks he is wise in this age, he should become a fool, so that he may become wise. (3:18).
For the wisdom of this world is foolishness in God’s sight. As it is written: “He catches the wise in their craftiness.” (3:19).
And again, “The Lord knows that the thoughts of the wise are futile.” (3:20).
Therefore, stop boasting in men. All things are yours, (3:21).
whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas or the world or life or death or the present or the future. All of them belong to you, (3:22).
and you belong to Christ, and Christ belongs to God. (3:23).
crossRefs: Job 5:13: He catches the wise in their own craftiness.
Psalm 94:11: The LORD knows the thoughts of man, that they are a breath.
Isaiah 28:16: I am laying in Zion a stone, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation.
Malachi 3:2-3: He is like a refiner's fire; he sits as a refiner and purifier of silver.
Hebrews 5:12-14: You need milk, not solid food; solid food is for the mature, trained by practice.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אִוֶּלֶת (ʾiwelet), Greek: μωρία (mōrίa, NT), Aramaic: סכלותא (סכלותא)
translationNotes.note: Denotes foolishness or absurdity; Paul applies it to how the cross appears to unbelievers.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הֵיכָל / מִקְדָּשׁ (hēykāl / miqədāš), Greek: ναός (naόs, NT), Aramaic: הֵיכְלָא (הֵיכְלָא)
translationNotes.note: Refers to God’s dwelling place; Paul applies it to the gathered church.

translationNotes.original: Greek: ἀρχιτέκτων (architekton)
translationNotes.note: The architekton was the contractor who set out a building and directed the trades under him, not a designer at a desk. Corinth was rebuilt as a Roman colony by Julius Caesar in 44 BC, a century after Rome destroyed the old city, so the readers lived in a construction site and knew what a bad foundation cost. Paul takes the title in 3:10 and immediately hands the site over to whoever builds next.

translationNotes.original: Greek: μισθός (misthos) - ζημιόω (zemioo)
translationNotes.note: Both words in 3:14-15 are trade terms. Misthos is the wage a workman is paid for a finished job, and zemioo is to be fined or made to bear a loss, the penalty a builder took when his work failed inspection. The picture is a contractor settling up at the end of a job, paid for what stands and docked for what burns.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul rebukes the Corinthians for their immaturity and divisions over Paul and Apollos, explaining that both are merely servants through whom God works; he warns that their spiritual work will be tested by fire, reminds them they are God's temple, and instructs them not to boast in human leaders since all things belong to those who are in Christ.

stories.title: 📜 1 Corinthians 4
summaryBullets: So then, men ought to regard us as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. (4:1).
Now it is required of stewards that they be found faithful. (4:2).
I care very little, however, if I am judged by you or by any human court. In fact, I do not even judge myself. (4:3).
My conscience is clear, but that does not vindicate me. It is the Lord who judges me. (4:4).

Therefore judge nothing before the appointed time; wait until the Lord comes. He will bring to light what is hidden in darkness and will expose the motives of men’s hearts. At that time each will receive his praise from God. (4:5).

Brothers, I have applied these things to myself and Apollos for your benefit, so that you may learn from us not to go beyond what is written. Then you will not take pride in one man over another. (4:6).
For who makes you so superior? What do you have that you did not receive? And if you did receive it, why do you boast as though you did not? (4:7).
Already you have all you want. Already you have become rich. Without us, you have become kings. How I wish you really were kings, so that we might be kings with you! (4:8).

For it seems to me that God has displayed us apostles at the end of the procession, like prisoners appointed for death. We have become a spectacle to the whole world, to angels as well as to men. (4:9).
We are fools for Christ, but you are wise in Christ. We are weak, but you are strong. You are honored, but we are dishonored. (4:10).
To this very hour we are hungry and thirsty, we are poorly clothed, we are brutally treated, we are homeless. (4:11).
We work hard with our own hands. When we are vilified, we bless; when we are persecuted, we endure it; (4:12).
when we are slandered, we answer gently. Up to this moment we have become the scum of the earth, the refuse of the world. (4:13).
I am not writing this to shame you, but to warn you as my beloved children. (4:14).
Even if you have ten thousand guardians in Christ, you do not have many fathers; for in Christ Jesus I became your father through the gospel. (4:15).
Therefore I urge you to imitate me. (4:16).
That is why I have sent you Timothy, my beloved and faithful child in the Lord. He will remind you of my way of life in Christ Jesus, which is exactly what I teach everywhere in every church. (4:17).
Some of you have become arrogant, as if I were not coming to you. (4:18).
But I will come to you shortly, if the Lord is willing, and then I will find out not only what these arrogant people are saying, but what power they have. (4:19).
For the kingdom of God is not a matter of talk but of power. (4:20).
Which do you prefer? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and with a gentle spirit? (4:21).
crossRefs: Luke 12:42-44: The faithful and wise steward set over the household to give out the food at the proper time.
Psalm 143:2: Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no one living is righteous before you.
Romans 2:29: The praise that counts comes from God, not from men.
Lamentations 3:45: You have made us scum and refuse among the peoples.
2 Corinthians 6:4-10: Paul's own list of what this service looks like: beatings, imprisonments, hunger, sleepless nights, having nothing and possessing everything.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אִוֶּלֶת (ʾiwelet), Greek: μωρία (mōrίa, NT), Aramaic: סכלותא (סכלותא)
translationNotes.note: Denotes foolishness or absurdity; Paul applies it to how the cross appears to unbelievers.

Ten thousand; also used idiomatically for 'countless.' Revelation 5:11's 'ten thousands of ten thousands' (myriades myriadon) of angels could be 100 million as a literal floor, though the intent is more naturally read as 'innumerable.'
translationNotes.original: Greek: μυριάς (myrias)
Greek: οἰκονόμος (oikonomos)
translationNotes.note: The household manager, in most large houses a slave himself. He held the keys, ran the estate, paid the workers and kept the accounts, and he owned none of it. That is the force of 4:2, that a steward must be found faithful: he answers to the owner, not to the household. Luke 16:1-8 turns on the same office, and the English word economy comes from the title.

translationNotes.term: A spectacle to the whole world
translationNotes.original: Greek: θέατρον (theatron)
translationNotes.note: Theatron is the theater, and by extension the show put on in it. Paul says God displayed the apostles at the end of the procession, like prisoners appointed for death, at 4:9. In a Roman triumph the condemned captives came last and were executed when it ended. Corinth was a Roman colony with its own theater, and Paul reaches for the games again at 1 Corinthians 9:24-27.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul instructs the Corinthians to view apostles as faithful stewards of God's mysteries, warns against premature judgment, and contrasts the apostles' suffering and hardship with the Corinthians' comfort and arrogance. He announces that Timothy is coming to remind them of his ways, threatens to visit soon with either discipline or gentleness, and asserts that God's kingdom operates through power, not mere words.

stories.title: ⚖️ 1 Corinthians 5
summaryBullets: It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and of a kind that is intolerable even among pagans: A man has his father’s wife. (5:1).
And you are proud! Shouldn’t you rather have been stricken with grief and have removed from your fellowship the man who did this? (5:2).
Although I am absent from you in body, I am present with you in spirit, and I have already pronounced judgment on the one who did this, just as if I were present. (5:3).
When you are assembled in the name of our Lord Jesus and I am with you in spirit, along with the power of the Lord Jesus, (5:4).
hand this man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved on the Day of the Lord. (5:5).
Your boasting is not good. Do you not know that a little leaven works through the whole batch of dough? (5:6).
Get rid of the old leaven, that you may be a new unleavened batch, as you really are. For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed. (5:7).
Therefore let us keep the feast, not with the old bread, leavened with malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and of truth. (5:8).
I wrote you in my letter not to associate with sexually immoral people. (5:9).
I was not including the sexually immoral of this world, or the greedy and swindlers, or idolaters. In that case you would have to leave this world. (5:10).

But now I am writing you not to associate with anyone who claims to be a brother but is sexually immoral or greedy, an idolater or a verbal abuser, a drunkard or a swindler. With such a man do not even eat. (5:11).
What business of mine is it to judge those outside the church? Are you not to judge those inside? (5:12).
God will judge those outside. “Expel the wicked man from among you.” (5:13).
crossRefs: Leviticus 18:8: Prohibition of uncovering father’s wife’s nakedness.
Deuteronomy 17:7: Purge the evil from your midst.
Galatians 5:9: A little leaven leavens the whole lump.
Exodus 12:21: Passover lamb sacrificed.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֵשֶׁת אָב (ʾēšet ʾāb), Greek: γυναῖκα τοῦ πατρός (gynaῖka toῦ patrόs, NT), Aramaic: אתת אבא (אתת אבא)
translationNotes.note: Refers to a stepmother; prohibited relationship in Leviticus 18:8 and Deuteronomy 22:30.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נָתַן לְשָׂטָן (nātan ləšāṭān, sense), Greek: παραδοῦναι τῷ Σατανᾷ (paradoῦnai tῷ Satanᾷ, NT), Aramaic: מסר לשטן (מסר לשטן)
translationNotes.note: Phrase for expelling from the protective sphere of the church, exposing the offender to consequences.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חָמֵץ (ḥāmēṣ), Greek: ζύμη (zύmē, NT), Aramaic: חמיעא (חמיעא)
translationNotes.note: Symbol of corruption spreading through the whole community.

translationNotes.original: Greek: ἔθνη (ethne), the nations
translationNotes.note: Paul says in 5:1 that this case would shock the pagans, and he is stating a legal fact, not exaggerating. Roman law barred a man from marrying his stepmother as firmly as Leviticus 18:8 and Deuteronomy 22:30 do, and a Roman court would have treated the union as void. So the church was tolerating something the surrounding city would have prosecuted, which is why Paul's reply in 5:2 is that they were proud of it.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul rebukes the Corinthians for tolerating sexual immorality, instructing them to remove the offender and maintain holiness in the community.

stories.title: ⚖️ 1 Corinthians 6
summaryBullets: If any of you has a grievance against another, how dare he go to law before the unrighteous instead of before the saints! (6:1).
Do you not know that the saints will judge the world? And if you are to judge the world, are you not competent to judge trivial cases? (6:2).
Do you not know that we will judge angels? How much more the things of this life! (6:3).
So if you need to settle everyday matters, do you appoint as judges those of no standing in the church? (6:4).
I say this to your shame. Is there really no one among you wise enough to arbitrate between his brothers? (6:5).
Instead, one brother goes to law against another, and this in front of unbelievers! (6:6).
The very fact that you have lawsuits among you means that you are thoroughly defeated already. Why not rather be wronged? Why not rather be cheated? (6:7).
Instead, you yourselves cheat and do wrong, even against your own brothers! (6:8).

Do you not know that the wicked will not inherit the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived: Neither the sexually immoral, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor men who submit to or perform homosexual acts, (6:9).
nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor verbal abusers, nor swindlers, will inherit the kingdom of God. (6:10).
And that is what some of you were. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God. (6:11).
“Everything is permissible for me,” but not everything is beneficial. “Everything is permissible for me,” but I will not be mastered by anything. (6:12).
“Food for the stomach and the stomach for food,” but God will destroy them both. The body is not intended for sexual immorality, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body. (6:13).
By His power God raised the Lord from the dead, and He will raise us also. (6:14).
Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I then take the members of Christ and unite them with a prostitute? Never! (6:15).
Or don’t you know that he who unites himself with a prostitute is one with her in body? For it is said, “The two will become one flesh.” (6:16).
But he who unites himself with the Lord is one with Him in spirit. (6:17).
Flee from sexual immorality. Every other sin a man can commit is outside his body, but he who sins sexually sins against his own body. (6:18).
Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have received from God? You are not your own; (6:19).
you were bought at a price. Therefore glorify God with your body. (6:20).
crossRefs: Matthew 19:28: Apostles will judge the twelve tribes.
Daniel 7:22: Saints receive the kingdom and judge.
Leviticus 18:22: Man shall not lie with man.
Galatians 5:19-21: Works of the flesh vice list.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: זוֹנִים (zōnîm), Greek: πόρνοι (pornoi, NT), Aramaic: זנאי (זנאי)
translationNotes.note: General term for those engaged in sexual immorality outside marriage.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מְרֻכָּכִים (sense, effeminate), Greek: μαλακοί (malakoi, NT), Aramaic: מַלָּכִין (מַלָּכִין)
translationNotes.note: Literally 'soft ones'; historically used for effeminate males or passive partners in male-male intercourse.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִשְׁכַּב זָכָר (Lev 18:22 phrase), Greek: ἀρσενοκοῖται (arsenokoitai, NT), Aramaic: דמִשְׁכַּב דִּכְרָא (דמִשְׁכַּב דִּכְרָא)
translationNotes.note: Coined directly from LXX Leviticus, 'male-bed'; refers to men who engage in sexual intercourse with men as active partners.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מְחָרֵף (məḥārēp, sense), Greek: λοίδοροι (loίdoroi, NT), Aramaic: מְחַסֵּף (מְחַסֵּף)
translationNotes.note: Verbally abusive or slanderous people.

translationNotes.term: going to law before the unrighteous
translationNotes.original: Greek: βῆμα (bema), the raised platform a magistrate judged from
translationNotes.note: A civil suit in a Roman colony was heard in the open forum, on a raised stone platform, in front of whoever was standing around. The system openly favored rank: a man of standing could not easily be dragged to court by a social inferior, and juries were drawn from the propertied. So a lawsuit between two believers in Corinth meant one of them had the connections to bring it and the other did not. Acts 18:12-17 shows the same platform in use, with the proconsul Gallio hearing the charge against Paul and then throwing it out.

translationNotes.term: Where Paul's word arsenokoitai comes from
translationNotes.original: Greek (LXX) Leviticus 18:22: μετὰ ἄρσενος οὐ κοιμηθήσῃ κοίτην γυναικός - Greek (LXX) Leviticus 20:13: ὃς ἂν κοιμηθῇ μετὰ ἄρσενος κοίτην γυναικός - Greek: ἀρσενοκοῖται (arsenokoitai), singular ἀρσενοκοίτης (arsenokoites)
translationNotes.note: Paul's word arsenokoitai, at 1 Corinthians 6:9 and 1 Timothy 1:10, means men who lie with males. Literally it is male-bedders: men who engage in sexual acts with other males. Koite is the ordinary Greek word for a bed and the standard term for sexual intercourse, which is how the New Testament itself uses it at Romans 13:13 and Hebrews 13:4. The word is a rare compound, and its two halves stand side by side in the Greek Old Testament of two verses: Leviticus 18:22 reads meta arsenos ou koimethese koiten gynaikos, and Leviticus 20:13 reads hos an koimethe meta arsenos koiten gynaikos, where arsenos and koiten are adjacent.

translationNotes.original: Greek: μαλακοί (malakoi), from μαλακός (malakos), soft
translationNotes.note: Malakos means soft. Its ordinary use is physical: Matthew 11:8 and Luke 7:25 both use it of fine clothing, a man dressed in soft garments in a king's house. In the list at 1 Corinthians 6:9 it stands directly before arsenokoitai, and in that pairing it denotes the one who takes the passive part in sexual acts between males while arsenokoitai denotes the active. Paul sets both in the same list, along with the sexually immoral, idolaters, adulterers, thieves, the greedy, drunkards, revilers, and swindlers.

translationNotes.original: Greek: ναός (naos), the inner sanctuary - ἱερόν (hieron), the temple complex
translationNotes.note: Greek has two words for the temple and 1 Corinthians 6:19 uses the narrower one. Hieron covers the whole precinct, courts and colonnades and all; Mark 11:15 uses it twice for the ground Jesus clears of traders. Naos is the sanctuary building itself, the room the presence occupied, which no ordinary worshipper entered. Naos is the word Paul puts on the body of the believer here, and he had already put it on the assembly at 1 Corinthians 3:16.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul shames believers for taking lawsuits before the unrighteous when the saints will judge the world, and lists the wicked who will not inherit God’s kingdom, though some were washed, sanctified, and justified; the body is for the Lord, a temple of the Holy Spirit bought at a price, so flee sexual immorality and glorify God with your body.

headings.text: The Temple of the Holy Spirit

stories.title: 🌿 1 Corinthians 7
summaryBullets: Now for the matters you wrote about: It is good to abstain from sexual relations. (7:1).
But because there is so much sexual immorality, each man should have his own wife, and each woman her own husband. (7:2).
The husband should fulfill his marital duty to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband. (7:3).
The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife. (7:4).

Do not deprive each other, except by mutual consent and for a time, so you may devote yourselves to prayer. Then come together again, so that Satan will not tempt you through your lack of self-control. (7:5).
I say this as a concession, not as a command. (7:6).
I wish that all men were as I am. But each man has his own gift from God; one has this gift, another has that. (7:7).
Now to the unmarried and widows I say this: It is good for them to remain unmarried, as I am. (7:8).
But if they cannot control themselves, let them marry. For it is better to marry than to burn with passion. (7:9).
To the married I give this command (not I, but the Lord): A wife must not separate from her husband. (7:10).
But if she does, she must remain unmarried or else be reconciled to her husband. And a husband must not divorce his wife. (7:11).
To the rest I say this (I, not the Lord): If a brother has an unbelieving wife and she is willing to live with him, he must not divorce her. (7:12).
And if a woman has an unbelieving husband and he is willing to live with her, she must not divorce him. (7:13).

For the unbelieving husband is sanctified through his believing wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified through her believing husband. Otherwise your children would be unclean, but now they are holy. (7:14).
But if the unbeliever leaves, let him go. The believing brother or sister is not bound in such cases. God has called you to live in peace. (7:15).
How do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife? (7:16).
Regardless, each one should lead the life that the Lord has assigned to him and to which God has called him. This is what I prescribe in all the churches. (7:17).
Was a man already circumcised when he was called? He should not become uncircumcised. Was a man still uncircumcised when called? He should not be circumcised. (7:18).
Circumcision is nothing and uncircumcision is nothing. Keeping God’s commandments is what counts. (7:19).
Each one should remain in the situation he was in when he was called. (7:20).
Were you a slave when you were called? Do not let it concern you— but if you can gain your freedom, take the opportunity. (7:21).
For he who was a slave when he was called by the Lord is the Lord’s freedman. Conversely, he who was a free man when he was called is Christ’s slave. (7:22).
You were bought at a price; do not become slaves of men. (7:23).
Brothers, each one should remain in the situation he was in when God called him. (7:24).
Now about virgins, I have no command from the Lord, but I give a judgment as one who by the Lord’s mercy is trustworthy. (7:25).
Because of the present crisis, I think it is good for a man to remain as he is. (7:26).
Are you committed to a wife? Do not seek to be released. Are you free of commitment? Do not look for a wife. (7:27).
But if you do marry, you have not sinned. And if a virgin marries, she has not sinned. But those who marry will face troubles in this life, and I want to spare you this. (7:28).
What I am saying, brothers, is that the time is short. From now on those who have wives should live as if they had none; (7:29).
those who weep, as if they did not; those who are joyful, as if they were not; those who make a purchase, as if they had nothing; (7:30).
and those who use the things of this world, as if not dependent on them. For this world in its present form is passing away. (7:31).
I want you to be free from concern. The unmarried man is concerned about the work of the Lord, how he can please the Lord. (7:32).
But the married man is concerned about the affairs of this world, how he can please his wife, (7:33).

and his interests are divided. The unmarried woman or virgin is concerned about the work of the Lord, how she can be holy in both body and spirit. But the married woman is concerned about the affairs of this world, how she can please her husband. (7:34).
I am saying this for your own good, not to restrict you, but in order to promote proper decorum and undivided devotion to the Lord. (7:35).

However, if someone thinks he is acting inappropriately toward his betrothed, and if she is beyond her youth and they ought to marry, let him do as he wishes; he is not sinning; they should get married. (7:36).
But the man who is firmly established in his heart and under no constraint, with control over his will and resolve in his heart not to marry the virgin, he will do well. (7:37).
So then, he who marries the virgin does well, but he who does not marry her does even better. (7:38).
A wife is bound to her husband as long as he lives. But if her husband dies, she is free to marry anyone she wishes, as long as he belongs to the Lord. (7:39).
In my judgment, however, she is happier if she remains as she is. And I think that I too have the Spirit of God. (7:40).
crossRefs: Genesis 2:24: Man shall leave father and mother and hold fast to wife.
Matthew 5:32: Jesus on divorce and remarriage.
Malachi 2:16: God hates divorce.
Acts 15:20: Instruction regarding Gentiles and sexual immorality.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֹנָה (ʿōnāh), Greek: τὴν ὀφειλήν (tὴn ὀpheilήn, NT), Aramaic: חובתא (חובתא)
translationNotes.note: Refers to marital duty of sexual relations owed between spouses.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לִבְעֹר בְּתַאֲוָה (libəʿōr bətaʾăwāh, sense), Greek: πυροῦσθαι (pyroῦsthai, NT), Aramaic: אתלהט בתאוותא (אתלהט בתאוותא)
translationNotes.note: Metaphor for uncontrolled sexual desire; marriage given as proper outlet.

translationNotes.term: If you can gain your freedom
translationNotes.original: Greek: ἀπελεύθερος (apeleutheros) - ἐξαγοράζω (exagorazo)
translationNotes.note: Slavery in the Roman world had exits. A master could free a slave in his will or by a formal act before a magistrate, and a slave could buy himself out with the peculium, the savings his master allowed him to keep; freed formally by a citizen owner, he became a citizen himself, though he still owed his old master set duties as a patron. At Delphi thousands of slaves were freed by a legal fiction in which the god Apollo bought them, and the contracts are cut into the temple wall. That is the world of 7:21-23, where Paul says the Lord's freedman is Christ's slave, and 'you were bought with a price'.

translationNotes.original: Greek: παρθένος (parthenos) - γαμίζω (gamizo)
translationNotes.note: Betrothal was not an engagement in the modern sense. It was a binding contract that made the couple husband and wife in law before they lived together, so breaking it required a divorce; that is why Joseph, betrothed to Mary, plans to divorce her quietly in Matthew 1:18-19. Girls were commonly betrothed young and the fathers made the agreement, which is the setting of 7:36-38, where the man deciding is the one with authority over the marriage.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul gives instructions on marriage, celibacy, and staying in one’s calling, emphasizing holiness, peace, and faithfulness.

stories.title: 📜 1 Corinthians 8
summaryBullets: Now about food sacrificed to idols: We know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up. (8:1).
The one who thinks he knows something does not yet know as he ought to know. (8:2).
But the one who loves God is known by God. (8:3).
So about eating food sacrificed to idols: We know that an idol is nothing at all in the world, and that there is no God but one. (8:4).
For even if there are so-called gods, whether in heaven or on earth (as there are many so-called gods and lords), (8:5).
yet for us there is but one God, the Father, from whom all things came and for whom we exist. And there is but one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things came and through whom we exist. (8:6).

But not everyone has this knowledge. Some people are still so accustomed to idols that they eat such food as if it were sacrificed to an idol. And since their conscience is weak, it is defiled. (8:7).
But food does not bring us closer to God: We are no worse if we do not eat, and no better if we do. (8:8).
Be careful, however, that your freedom does not become a stumbling block to the weak. (8:9).
For if someone with a weak conscience sees you who are well informed eating in an idol’s temple, will he not be encouraged to eat food sacrificed to idols? (8:10).
So this weak brother, for whom Christ died, is destroyed by your knowledge. (8:11).
By sinning against your brothers in this way and wounding their weak conscience, you sin against Christ. (8:12).
Therefore, if what I eat causes my brother to stumble, I will never eat meat again, so that I will not cause him to stumble. (8:13).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 6:4: The Lord is one.
Psalm 24:1: The earth is the Lord’s.
Romans 14:20-21: Do not destroy the work of God for food.
1 Thessalonians 5:11: Build one another up.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: זִבְחֵי אֱלִילִים (zibəḥēy ʾĕliyliym), Greek: εἰδωλόθυτα (eἰdōlόthyta, NT), Aramaic: דבחי פסילי (דבחי פסילי)
translationNotes.note: Refers to meat from sacrifices in pagan temples; a major issue in Corinth with social and religious implications.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִכְשׁוֹל (mikəšwōl), Greek: πρόσκομμα (prόskomma, NT), Aramaic: תקלא (תקלא)
translationNotes.note: Figurative for something that causes another to fall spiritually.

translationNotes.term: At table in an idol's temple
translationNotes.original: Greek: ἐν εἰδωλείῳ κατακείμενον (en eidoleio katakeimenon)
translationNotes.note: Ancient temples were catering halls as well as places of sacrifice. The sanctuary of Asklepios at Corinth had dining rooms with stone couches built in, and the invitations survive: one Egyptian papyrus reads, 'Chairemon invites you to dine at the table of the lord Serapis in the Serapeion tomorrow, the fifteenth, at the ninth hour.' Guild dinners, weddings and civic feasts were all held on temple ground, so a believer who refused them lost his business and social life at once. That is the scene in 8:10.

translationNotes.term: Quoting the Corinthians back to themselves
translationNotes.original: Greek: γνῶσις (gnosis)
translationNotes.note: Ancient Greek was written without quotation marks, so a translator has to decide where a quoted line stops. Several short sentences here read as slogans of the Corinthians that Paul repeats before answering: 'all of us possess knowledge' (8:1), 'an idol is nothing in the world' and 'there is no God but one' (8:4). Modern versions put some of them in quotation marks and some do not, and that is an editorial judgment, not something the Greek marks.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul affirms idols are nothing and food is indifferent, but insists that love must govern knowledge, avoiding stumbling of the weak.

stories.title: 📜 1 Corinthians 9
summaryBullets: Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus our Lord? Are you yourselves not my workmanship in the Lord? (9:1).
Even if I am not an apostle to others, surely I am to you. For you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord. (9:2).
This is my defense to those who scrutinize me: (9:3).
Have we no right to food and to drink? (9:4).
Have we no right to take along a believing wife, as do the other apostles and the Lord’s brothers and Cephas? (9:5).
Or are Barnabas and I the only apostles who must work for a living? (9:6).
Who serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Who tends a flock and does not drink of its milk? (9:7).
Do I say this from a human perspective? Doesn’t the Law say the same thing? (9:8).
For it is written in the Law of Moses: “Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain.” Is it about oxen that God is concerned? (9:9).
Isn’t He actually speaking on our behalf? Indeed, this was written for us, because when the plowman plows and the thresher threshes, they should also expect to share in the harvest. (9:10).
If we have sown spiritual seed among you, is it too much for us to reap a material harvest from you? (9:11).
If others have this right to your support, shouldn’t we have it all the more? But we did not exercise this right. Instead, we put up with anything rather than hinder the gospel of Christ. (9:12).
Do you not know that those who work in the temple eat of its food, and those who serve at the altar partake of its offerings? (9:13).
In the same way, the Lord has prescribed that those who preach the gospel should receive their living from the gospel. (9:14).
But I have not used any of these rights. And I am not writing this to suggest that something be done for me. Indeed, I would rather die than let anyone nullify my boast. (9:15).
Yet when I preach the gospel, I have no reason to boast, because I am obligated to preach. Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel! (9:16).
If my preaching is voluntary, I have a reward. But if it is not voluntary, I am still entrusted with a responsibility. (9:17).
What then is my reward? That in preaching the gospel I may offer it free of charge, and so not use up my rights in preaching it. (9:18).
Though I am free of obligation to anyone, I make myself a slave to everyone, to win as many as possible. (9:19).
To the Jews I became like a Jew, to win the Jews. To those under the law I became like one under the law (though I myself am not under the law), to win those under the law. (9:20).
To those without the law I became like one without the law (though I am not outside the law of God but am under the law of Christ), to win those without the law. (9:21).
To the weak I became weak, to win the weak. I have become all things to all people so that by all possible means I might save some. (9:22).
I do all this for the sake of the gospel, so that I may share in its blessings. (9:23).
Do you not know that in a race all the runners run, but only one receives the prize? Run in such a way as to take the prize. (9:24).
Everyone who competes in the games trains with strict discipline. They do it for a crown that is perishable, but we do it for a crown that is imperishable. (9:25).
Therefore I do not run aimlessly; I do not fight like I am beating the air. (9:26).
No, I discipline my body and make it my slave, so that after I have preached to others, I myself will not be disqualified. (9:27).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 25:4: Do not muzzle an ox while treading out grain.
Luke 10:7: The laborer deserves his wages.
Philippians 3:14: Press toward the prize of the upward call.
2 Timothy 4:7-8: The crown of righteousness.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֲטֶרֶת (ʿăṭeret, sense), Greek: στέφανος (stέphanos, NT), Aramaic: כלילא (כלילא)
translationNotes.note: Refers to a victor’s crown in athletic games; Paul contrasts perishable with imperishable reward.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נִמְאָס (niməʾās, sense), Greek: ἀδόκιμος (ἀdόkimos, NT), Aramaic: פסילא (פסילא)
translationNotes.note: Means rejected or failing the test; Paul applies it metaphorically to himself if undisciplined.

translationNotes.original: Greek: ἀγών (agon) - στάδιον (stadion)
translationNotes.note: Corinth ran the Isthmian Games at the sanctuary of Poseidon a few miles from the city, held every two years and second in prestige only to Olympia, so the crowd Paul is writing to had seen the events he describes. Competitors swore an oath and trained under supervision for months before they were allowed to enter; at Olympia the rule was ten months, the last of them on site. The prize was a wreath, at the Isthmus of wild celery and later of pine, and it was dead within days, which is the point of the perishable crown in 9:25.

translationNotes.original: Greek: ὑπωπιάζω (hypopiazo)
translationNotes.note: The verb in 9:27 means to strike under the eye, to give a man a black eye. Greek boxing had no rounds, no weight classes and no padded gloves; the fighters bound their hands with leather thongs and the bout ran until one man was down or lifted a finger to quit. Paul says he does not throw punches at nothing and that the body he is hitting is his own.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul explains his rights as an apostle but shows he renounces them for the gospel’s sake, illustrating with athletic discipline to win the prize.

stories.title: ⚖️ 1 Corinthians 10
summaryBullets: I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that our forefathers were all under the cloud, and that they all passed through the sea. (10:1).
They were all baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea. (10:2).
They all ate the same spiritual food (10:3).
and drank the same spiritual drink; for they drank from the spiritual rock that accompanied them, and that rock was Christ. (10:4).
Nevertheless, God was not pleased with most of them, for they were struck down in the wilderness. (10:5).
These things took place as examples to keep us from craving evil things as they did. (10:6).
Do not be idolaters, as some of them were. As it is written: “The people sat down to eat and drink and got up to indulge in revelry.” (10:7).
We should not commit sexual immorality, as some of them did, and in one day twenty-three thousand of them died. (10:8).
We should not test Christ, as some of them did, and were killed by snakes. (10:9).
And do not complain, as some of them did, and were killed by the destroying angel. (10:10).
Now these things happened to them as examples and were written down as warnings for us, on whom the fulfillment of the ages has come. (10:11).
So the one who thinks he is standing firm should be careful not to fall. (10:12).

No temptation has seized you except what is common to man. And God is faithful; He will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear. But when you are tempted, He will also provide an escape, so that you can stand up under it. (10:13).
Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry. (10:14).
I speak to reasonable people; judge for yourselves what I say. (10:15).
Is not the cup of blessing that we bless a participation in the blood of Christ? And is not the bread that we break a participation in the body of Christ? (10:16).
Because there is one loaf, we who are many are one body; for we all partake of the one loaf. (10:17).
Consider the people of Israel: Are not those who eat the sacrifices fellow partakers in the altar? (10:18).
Am I suggesting, then, that food sacrificed to an idol is anything, or that an idol is anything? (10:19).
No, but the sacrifices of pagans are offered to demons, not to God. And I do not want you to be participants with demons. (10:20).
You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons too; you cannot partake in the table of the Lord and the table of demons too. (10:21).
Are we trying to provoke the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than He? (10:22).
“Everything is permissible,” but not everything is beneficial. “Everything is permissible,” but not everything is edifying. (10:23).
No one should seek his own good, but the good of others. (10:24).
Eat anything sold in the meat market without raising questions of conscience, (10:25).
for, “The earth is the Lord’s, and the fullness thereof.” (10:26).
If an unbeliever invites you to a meal and you want to go, eat anything set before you without raising questions of conscience. (10:27).
But if someone tells you, “This food was offered to idols,” then do not eat it, for the sake of the one who told you and for the sake of conscience — (10:28).
the other one’s conscience, I mean, not your own. For why should my freedom be determined by someone else’s conscience? (10:29).
If I partake in the meal with thankfulness, why am I denounced because of that for which I give thanks? (10:30).
So whether you eat or drink or whatever you do, do it all to the glory of God. (10:31).
Do not become a stumbling block, whether to Jews or Greeks or the church of God— (10:32).
as I also try to please everyone in all I do. For I am not seeking my own good, but the good of many, that they may be saved. (10:33).
crossRefs: Exodus 32:6: The people sat down to eat and drink and rose to play.
Numbers 25:1-9: Israel’s immorality at Baal of Peor.
Numbers 21:6: Serpents sent among the people.
Deuteronomy 32:17: Sacrifices offered to demons.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נָפַל (nāpal, sense), Greek: κατεστρώθησαν (katestrώthēsan, NT), Aramaic: נפיל (נפיל)
translationNotes.note: Means struck down or laid low; describes Israel’s death in wilderness.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כּוֹס בְּרָכָה (kwōs bərākāh), Greek: ποτήριον τῆς εὐλογίας (potήrion tῆs eὐlogίas, NT), Aramaic: כסא דבִרכָתא (כסא דבִרכָתא)
translationNotes.note: Name for cup used in Jewish meal blessing; Paul applies it to the Lord’s Supper.

translationNotes.original: Greek: μάκελλον (makellon)
translationNotes.note: Makellon is Greek borrowing the Latin word macellum, the city's covered market for meat and fish. Much of what hung there had come off a temple altar, since the priests' share of a sacrifice was sold on for cash. Pliny the Younger, writing to the emperor Trajan about AD 112, reports that sacrificial meat had lately found almost no buyers where the Christians had spread, which shows the trade was real and that believers were known for avoiding it. Paul's ruling in 10:25 is to buy and eat without cross-examining the butcher.

translationNotes.original: Greek: κοινωνία (koinonia) - κοινωνός (koinonos)
translationNotes.note: Koinonia is having a thing in common, and it was ordinary commercial language: koinonoi were business partners, which is exactly what Luke 5:10 calls James and John in Simon's fishing concern. In 10:16-21 Paul uses it of the cup and the bread, and then of the table of demons, and the force is joint ownership, not warm feeling. English 'fellowship' and 'communion' both soften it.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul warns from Israel’s history not to fall into idolatry, immorality, or testing God, and affirms participation in the Lord’s table is incompatible with idolatry.

stories.title: 🌿 1 Corinthians 11
summaryBullets: You are to imitate me, just as I imitate Christ. (11:1).
Now I commend you for remembering me in everything and for maintaining the traditions, just as I passed them on to you. (11:2).
But I want you to understand that the head of every man is Christ, and the head of the woman is man, and the head of Christ is God. (11:3).
Every man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonors his head. (11:4).
And every woman who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonors her head, for it is just as if her head were shaved. (11:5).
If a woman does not cover her head, she should have her hair cut off. And if it is shameful for a woman to have her hair cut or shaved off, she should cover her head. (11:6).
A man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God; but the woman is the glory of man. (11:7).
For man did not come from woman, but woman from man. (11:8).
Neither was man created for woman, but woman for man. (11:9).
For this reason a woman ought to have a sign of authority on her head, because of the angels. (11:10).
In the Lord, however, woman is not independent of man, nor is man independent of woman. (11:11).
For just as woman came from man, so also man is born of woman. But everything comes from God. (11:12).
Judge for yourselves: Is it proper for a woman to pray to God with her head uncovered? (11:13).
Doesn’t nature itself teach you that if a man has long hair, it is a disgrace to him, (11:14).
but that if a woman has long hair, it is her glory? For long hair is given to her as a covering. (11:15).
If anyone is inclined to dispute this, we have no other practice, nor do the churches of God. (11:16).
In the following instructions I have no praise to offer, because your gatherings do more harm than good. (11:17).
First of all, I hear that when you come together as a church, there are divisions among you, and in part I believe it. (11:18).
And indeed, there must be differences among you to show which of you are approved. (11:19).
Now then, when you come together, it is not the Lord’s Supper you eat. (11:20).
For as you eat, each of you goes ahead without sharing his meal. While one remains hungry, another gets drunk. (11:21).

Don’t you have your own homes in which to eat and drink? Or do you despise the church of God and humiliate those who have nothing? What can I say to you? Shall I praise you for this? No, I will not! (11:22).
For I received from the Lord what I also passed on to you: The Lord Jesus, on the night He was betrayed, took bread, (11:23).
and when He had given thanks, He broke it and said, [J]“This is My body, which is for you; do this in remembrance of Me.”[/J] (11:24).
In the same way, after supper He took the cup, saying, [J]“This cup is the new covenant in My blood; do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of Me.”[/J] (11:25).
For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until He comes. (11:26).
Therefore, whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty of sinning against the body and blood of the Lord. (11:27).
Each one must examine himself before he eats of the bread and drinks of the cup. (11:28).
For anyone who eats and drinks without recognizing the body eats and drinks judgment on himself. (11:29).
That is why many among you are weak and sick, and a number of you have fallen asleep. (11:30).
Now if we judged ourselves properly, we would not come under judgment. (11:31).
But when we are judged by the Lord, we are being disciplined so that we will not be condemned with the world. (11:32).
So, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another. (11:33).
If anyone is hungry, he should eat at home, so that when you come together it will not result in judgment. And when I come, I will give instructions about the remaining matters. (11:34).
crossRefs: Psalm 24:1: The earth is the Lord’s.
Romans 14:20-21: Do not destroy the work of God for food.
Philippians 2:4: Look to the interests of others.
Colossians 3:17: Do all in the name of the Lord.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַצְפּוּן (maṣəpwn, sense), Greek: συνείδησις (syneίdēsis, NT), Aramaic: תֵּאוּת דְּלִבָּא (תֵּאוּת דְּלִבָּא)
translationNotes.note: Inner faculty of moral awareness; Paul emphasizes sensitivity to another’s conscience, not just one’s own.

translationNotes.original: Greek: κατὰ κεφαλῆς ἔχων (kata kephales echon)
translationNotes.note: Corinth was a Roman colony and its leading men dressed Roman. A Roman of rank pulled a fold of his toga over his head when he sacrificed or prayed, capite velato, and the statues show it; Greek men sacrificed bareheaded. A respectable married woman appeared in public with her head covered, and going out uncovered was read as a statement about her status. Both halves of 11:4-16 are aimed at a room where those signals were obvious and are invisible to us.

translationNotes.original: Greek: δεῖπνον (deipnon)
translationNotes.note: A dining room was a triclinium, three couches around a table, seating about nine; everyone else ate in the courtyard. Hosts commonly graded the food and wine by the rank of the guest: Pliny the Younger describes a dinner where the best wine went to the host and his friends and the cheapest to the freedmen (Letters 2.6), and Martial mocks the same practice in his epigrams. The wealthy also arrived early because they set their own hours while workers and slaves could not. That is the machinery behind 11:20-22, where one is hungry and another is drunk.

translationNotes.original: Greek: κοιμάομαι (koimaomai)
translationNotes.note: The verb means to fall asleep, and 11:30 uses it plainly for believers who have died. Greek built the noun koimeterion on it, a sleeping place, which passed through Latin into English as 'cemetery'. Paul uses the same word all through 15:6-20 for the dead in Christ.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul teaches on headship and coverings for praying and prophesying, man being the image and glory of God and woman the glory of man, though in the Lord neither is independent of the other; he rebukes divisions at their meals, recounts the Lord’s Supper instituted on the night Jesus was betrayed, and commands self-examination, for eating and drinking unworthily brings judgment.

stories.title: 🌿 1 Corinthians 12
summaryBullets: Now about spiritual gifts, brothers, I do not want you to be uninformed. (12:1).
You know that when you were pagans, you were influenced and led astray to mute idols. (12:2).
Therefore I inform you that no one who is speaking by the Spirit of God says, “Jesus be cursed,” and no one can say, “Jesus is Lord,” except by the Holy Spirit. (12:3).
There are different gifts, but the same Spirit. (12:4).
There are different ministries, but the same Lord. (12:5).
There are different ways of working, but the same God works all things in all people. (12:6).
Now to each one the manifestation of the Spirit is given for the common good. (12:7).
To one there is given through the Spirit the message of wisdom, to another the message of knowledge by the same Spirit, (12:8).
to another faith by the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing by that one Spirit, (12:9).

to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another distinguishing between spirits, to another speaking in various tongues, and to still another the interpretation of tongues. (12:10).
All these are the work of one and the same Spirit, who apportions them to each one as He determines. (12:11).
The body is a unit, though it is composed of many parts. And although its parts are many, they all form one body. So it is with Christ. (12:12).
For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, slave or free, and we were all given one Spirit to drink. (12:13).
For the body does not consist of one part, but of many. (12:14).
If the foot should say, “Because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body,” that would not make it any less a part of the body. (12:15).
And if the ear should say, “Because I am not an eye, I do not belong to the body,” that would not make it any less a part of the body. (12:16).
If the whole body were an eye, where would the sense of hearing be? If the whole body were an ear, where would the sense of smell be? (12:17).
But in fact, God has arranged the members of the body, every one of them, according to His design. (12:18).
If they were all one part, where would the body be? (12:19).
As it is, there are many parts, but one body. (12:20).
The eye cannot say to the hand, “I do not need you.” Nor can the head say to the feet, “I do not need you.” (12:21).
On the contrary, the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable, (12:22).
and the parts we consider less honorable, we treat with greater honor. And our unpresentable parts are treated with special modesty, (12:23).
whereas our presentable parts have no such need. But God has composed the body and has given greater honor to the parts that lacked it, (12:24).
so that there should be no division in the body, but that its members should have mutual concern for one another. (12:25).
If one part suffers, every part suffers with it; if one part is honored, every part rejoices with it. (12:26).
Now you are the body of Christ, and each of you is a member of it. (12:27).

And in the church God has appointed first of all apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then workers of miracles, and those with gifts of healing, helping, administration, and various tongues. (12:28).
Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Do all work miracles? (12:29).
Do all have gifts of healing? Do all speak in tongues? Do all interpret? (12:30).
But eagerly desire the greater gifts. And now I will show you the most excellent way. (12:31).
crossRefs: Romans 12:4-8: One body, many members, differing gifts.
Ephesians 4:11-13: Apostles, prophets, teachers given for building up.
John 7:37-39: Drink of the Spirit.
Galatians 3:28: Neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַתָּנוֹת (matānwōt), Greek: χαρίσματα (charίsmata, NT), Aramaic: מתנתא (מתנתא)
translationNotes.note: Charismata denotes gifts of grace given by the Spirit for service.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לָשׁוֹן (lāšōn), Greek: γλῶσσα (glōssa, NT), Aramaic: לִשָּׁן (lishān)
translationNotes.note: Literally “tongue, language.” In both Testaments it refers to real languages. In Acts 2, the Spirit enabled believers to speak foreign human languages understood by others. In 1 Corinthians 12-14, the same word describes Spirit-given speech that may require interpretation if not naturally understood. It is always real, meaningful communication; not nonsense syllables.

translationNotes.original: Greek: σῶμα (soma) - μέλος (melos)
translationNotes.note: The picture of a community as a body whose parts quarrel was a stock piece of ancient public speaking. Livy tells how Menenius Agrippa broke the plebeian walkout of 494 BC by telling the crowd the fable of the belly and the limbs, which downed tools against the stomach and starved themselves (History 2.32). The Corinthians would have recognized the figure at once, and would have noticed that Paul turns it the other way: his argument protects the parts the body calls weaker and less honorable (12:22-24).

translationNotes.original: Greek: ἀντίλημψις (antilempsis) - κυβέρνησις (kybernesis)
translationNotes.note: Two of the items in the list at 12:28 are hidden by their English labels. Antilempsis is built on a verb meaning to take hold of something in order to hold it up, the word used for helping the weak in Acts 20:35 and for God helping Israel in Luke 1:54. Kybernesis is the steersman's work: a kybernetes is the pilot of a ship, the man at the helm in Acts 27:11 and Revelation 18:17. The gifts are propping up and steering, not paperwork.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul explains spiritual gifts are diverse but from one Spirit, compares the church to a body with many members, and urges seeking the greater gifts in love.

stories.title: 🌿 1 Corinthians 13
summaryBullets: If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am only a ringing gong or a clanging cymbal. (13:1).
If I have the gift of prophecy and can fathom all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have absolute faith so as to move mountains, but have not love, I am nothing. (13:2).
If I give all I possess to the poor and exult in the surrender of my body, but have not love, I gain nothing. (13:3).
Love is patient, love is kind. It does not envy, it does not boast, it is not proud. (13:4).
It is not rude, it is not self-seeking, it is not easily angered, it keeps no account of wrongs. (13:5).
Love takes no pleasure in evil, but rejoices in the truth. (13:6).
It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. (13:7).
Love never fails. But where there are prophecies, they will cease; where there are tongues, they will be restrained; where there is knowledge, it will be dismissed. (13:8).
For we know in part and we prophesy in part, (13:9).
but when the perfect comes, the partial passes away. (13:10).
When I was a child, I talked like a child, I thought like a child, I reasoned like a child. When I became a man, I set aside childish ways. (13:11).
Now we see but a dim reflection as in a mirror; then we shall see face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I am fully known. (13:12).
And now these three remain: faith, hope, and love; but the greatest of these is love. (13:13).
crossRefs: John 13:35: By this all will know you are my disciples, if you love one another.
Colossians 3:14: Above all put on love, which binds everything together.
1 John 4:8: God is love.
Song of Songs 8:7: Many waters cannot quench love.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מְצִלְתַּיִם (məṣilətayim), Greek: κύμβαλον (kύmbalon, NT), Aramaic: צלצלא (צלצלא)
translationNotes.note: Instrument reference; metaphor for noise without substance.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַרְאָה (marəʾāh), Greek: ἐν αἰνίγματι (ἐn aἰnίgmati, NT), Aramaic: בחידתא (בחידתא)
translationNotes.note: Literally 'in an enigma'; Corinth was known for bronze mirrors, which gave dim reflection.

translationNotes.original: Greek: ἀγάπη (agape) - ἔρως (eros) - φιλία (philia)
translationNotes.note: Greek had several words English gives as love: eros for desire, philia for the affection of friends and kin, storge for family attachment, and agape, which was the least loaded of them. It is not a word that carries a high meaning on its own; the Greek Old Testament uses the same verb for Amnon's desire for Tamar in 2 Samuel 13:15. Paul fills it instead: 13:4-7 defines love with fifteen verbs, things it does and does not do, and not one adjective.

This chapter was not written as a set piece. It sits inside a single argument that runs from chapter 12 to chapter 14 about gifts in the assembly, and the break at 12:31 and 14:1 is a later editor's mark. Chapter divisions were added by Stephen Langton, Archbishop of Canterbury, about 1227, and verse numbers by the printer Robert Estienne in his Greek New Testament of 1551. Neither is part of the letter Paul dictated.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul describes love as greater than all gifts and enduring beyond them, essential for true Christian life.

stories.title: 📜 1 Corinthians 14
summaryBullets: Earnestly pursue love and eagerly desire spiritual gifts, especially the gift of prophecy. (14:1).
For he who speaks in a tongue does not speak to men, but to God. Indeed, no one understands him; he utters mysteries in the Spirit. (14:2).
But he who prophesies speaks to men for their edification, encouragement, and comfort. (14:3).
The one who speaks in a tongue edifies himself, but the one who prophesies edifies the church. (14:4).

I wish that all of you could speak in tongues, but I would rather have you prophesy. He who prophesies is greater than one who speaks in tongues, unless he interprets so that the church may be edified. (14:5).
Now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, how will I benefit you, unless I bring you some revelation or knowledge or prophecy or teaching? (14:6).
Even in the case of lifeless instruments, such as the flute or harp, how will anyone recognize the tune they are playing unless the notes are distinct? (14:7).
Again, if the trumpet sounds a muffled call, who will prepare for battle? (14:8).
So it is with you. Unless you speak intelligible words with your tongue, how will anyone know what you are saying? You will just be speaking into the air. (14:9).
Assuredly, there are many different languages in the world, yet none of them is without meaning. (14:10).
If, then, I do not know the meaning of someone’s language, I am a foreigner to the speaker, and he is a foreigner to me. (14:11).
It is the same with you. Since you are eager to have spiritual gifts, strive to excel in gifts that build up the church. (14:12).
Therefore, the one who speaks in a tongue should pray that he may interpret. (14:13).
For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind is unfruitful. (14:14).
What then shall I do? I will pray with my spirit, but I will also pray with my mind. I will sing with my spirit, but I will also sing with my mind. (14:15).
Otherwise, if you speak a blessing in spirit, how can someone who is uninstructed say “Amen” to your thanksgiving, since he does not know what you are saying? (14:16).
You may be giving thanks well enough, but the other one is not edified. (14:17).
I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you. (14:18).
But in the church, I would rather speak five coherent words to instruct others than ten thousand words in a tongue. (14:19).
Brothers, stop thinking like children. In regard to evil be infants, but in your thinking be mature. (14:20).
It is written in the Law: “By strange tongues and foreign lips I will speak to this people, but even then they will not listen to Me, says the Lord.” (14:21).
Tongues, then, are a sign, not for believers, but for unbelievers. Prophecy, however, is for believers, not for unbelievers. (14:22).
So if the whole church comes together and everyone speaks in tongues, and some who are uninstructed or some unbelievers come in, will they not say that you are out of your minds? (14:23).
But if an unbeliever or uninstructed person comes in while everyone is prophesying, he will be convicted and called to account by all, (14:24).
and the secrets of his heart will be made known. So he will fall facedown and worship God, proclaiming, “God is truly among you!” (14:25).
What then shall we say, brothers? When you come together, everyone has a psalm or a teaching, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation. All of these must be done to build up the church. (14:26).
If anyone speaks in a tongue, two, or at most three, should speak in turn, and someone must interpret. (14:27).
But if there is no interpreter, he should remain silent in the church and speak only to himself and God. (14:28).
Two or three prophets should speak, and the others should weigh carefully what is said. (14:29).
And if a revelation comes to someone who is seated, the first speaker should stop. (14:30).
For you can all prophesy in turn so that everyone may be instructed and encouraged. (14:31).
The spirits of prophets are subject to prophets. (14:32).
For God is not a God of disorder, but of peace— as in all the churches of the saints. (14:33).
Women are to be silent in the churches. They are not permitted to speak, but must be in submission, as the law says. (14:34).
If they wish to inquire about something, they are to ask their own husbands at home; for it is dishonorable for a woman to speak in the church. (14:35).
Did the word of God originate with you? Or are you the only ones it has reached? (14:36).
If anyone considers himself a prophet or spiritual person, let him acknowledge that what I am writing you is the Lord’s command. (14:37).
But if anyone ignores this, he himself will be ignored. (14:38).
So, my brothers, be eager to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues. (14:39).
But everything must be done in a proper and orderly manner. (14:40).
crossRefs: Isaiah 28:11-12: The passage Paul quotes at 14:21, where God speaks to this people by foreign tongues and mocking lips and still they will not listen.
1 Corinthians 11:5: Three chapters earlier in this same letter Paul writes of every woman who prays or prophesies, and what he corrects there is her head rather than her speaking.
Joel 2:28-29: The LORD promises to pour out His Spirit on all people so that sons and daughters prophesy, menservants and maidservants included.
Acts 21:9: Philip the evangelist had four unmarried daughters who prophesied, reported flatly in the same book that records Paul's year and a half at Corinth.
1 Thessalonians 5:19-21: Do not extinguish the Spirit or treat prophecies with contempt, but test all things, which is the weighing 14:29 hands to the assembly.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לָשׁוֹן (lāšwōn), Greek: γλῶσσα (glῶssa, NT), Aramaic: לִשָּׁן (לִשָּׁן)
translationNotes.note: Literally 'language'; may refer to human languages or ecstatic utterances.

translationNotes.original: Greek: σιγάω (sigao) - σιγάτω (sigato) - σιγάτωσαν (sigatosan)
translationNotes.note: One verb carries three separate commands within seven verses. At 14:28 a man speaking in a tongue with no interpreter is to keep silent in the church, sigato. At 14:30 the man already on his feet is to stop when a revelation comes to someone seated, sigato again. At 14:34 the women are to keep silent, sigatosan; and Paul frames the whole run at 14:33 with 'God is not a God of disorder, but of peace' and closes it at 14:40 with 'everything must be done in a proper and orderly manner'.

translationNotes.original: Greek: καθὼς καὶ ὁ νόμος λέγει (kathos kai ho nomos legei)
translationNotes.note: Paul appeals to the law at 14:34 without quoting it or naming the passage, which is not how he handles Scripture elsewhere in this letter. At 9:9 he writes 'it is written in the Law of Moses' and quotes Deuteronomy 25:4 about the ox; at 14:21 he writes 'it is written in the Law' and quotes Isaiah 28:11-12; at 15:54-55 he puts Isaiah 25:8 and Hosea 13:14 together word for word. At 14:34 he gives no text.

translationNotes.original: Greek: προφητεύω (propheteuo)
translationNotes.note: Prophecy is the thing this chapter pushes the assembly toward from beginning to end. 14:1 tells them to desire it above every other gift, 14:24-25 pictures an unbeliever walking in while everyone is prophesying and falling on his face, 14:31 says 'you can all prophesy in turn so that everyone may be instructed and encouraged', and 14:39 closes 'be eager to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues'. Paul has already written in this letter of women praying and prophesying (11:5).

translationNotes.original: Greek: μυριάς (myrias)
translationNotes.note: Ten thousand; also used idiomatically for 'countless.' Revelation 5:11's 'ten thousands of ten thousands' (myriades myriadon) of angels could be 100 million as a literal floor, though the intent is more naturally read as 'innumerable.'

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul contrasts prophecy and tongues, urging orderly worship, building up the church, and submission to the Lord’s command.

stories.title: 🌅 1 Corinthians 15
summaryBullets: Now, brothers, I want to remind you of the gospel I preached to you, which you received, and in which you stand firm. (15:1).
By this gospel you are saved, if you hold firmly to the word I preached to you. Otherwise, you have believed in vain. (15:2).
For what I received I passed on to you as of first importance: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, (15:3).
that He was buried, that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, (15:4).
and that He appeared to Cephas and then to the Twelve. (15:5).
After that, He appeared to more than five hundred brothers at once, most of whom are still living, though some have fallen asleep. (15:6).
Then He appeared to James, then to all the apostles. (15:7).
And last of all He appeared to me also, as to one of untimely birth. (15:8).
For I am the least of the apostles and am unworthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God. (15:9).
But by the grace of God I am what I am, and His grace to me was not in vain. No, I worked harder than all of them — yet not I, but the grace of God that was with me. (15:10).
Whether, then, it was I or they, this is what we preach, and this is what you believed. (15:11).
But if it is preached that Christ has been raised from the dead, how can some of you say that there is no resurrection of the dead? (15:12).
If there is no resurrection of the dead, then not even Christ has been raised. (15:13).
And if Christ has not been raised, our preaching is worthless, and so is your faith. (15:14).

In that case, we are also exposed as false witnesses about God. For we have testified about God that He raised Christ from the dead, but He did not raise Him if in fact the dead are not raised. (15:15).
For if the dead are not raised, then not even Christ has been raised. (15:16).
And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile; you are still in your sins. (15:17).
Then those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished. (15:18).
If our hope in Christ is for this life alone, we are to be pitied more than all men. (15:19).
But Christ has indeed been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. (15:20).
For since death came through a man, the resurrection of the dead comes also through a man. (15:21).
For as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive. (15:22).
But each in his own turn: Christ the firstfruits; then at His coming, those who belong to Him. (15:23).
