Then the end will come, when He hands over the kingdom to God the Father after He has destroyed all dominion, authority, and power. (15:24).
For He must reign until He has put all His enemies under His feet. (15:25).
The last enemy to be destroyed is death. (15:26).
For “God has put everything under His feet.” Now when it says that everything has been put under Him, this clearly does not include the One who put everything under Him. (15:27).
And when all things have been subjected to Him, then the Son Himself will be made subject to Him who put all things under Him, so that God may be all in all. (15:28).
If these things are not so, what will those do who are baptized for the dead? If the dead are not raised at all, why are people baptized for them? (15:29).
And why do we endanger ourselves every hour? (15:30).
I face death every day, brothers, as surely as I boast about you in Christ Jesus our Lord. (15:31).
If I fought wild beasts in Ephesus for human motives, what did I gain? If the dead are not raised, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.” (15:32).
Do not be deceived: “Bad company corrupts good character.” (15:33).
Sober up as you ought, and stop sinning; for some of you are ignorant of God. I say this to your shame. (15:34).
But someone will ask, “How are the dead raised? With what kind of body will they come?” (15:35).
You fool! What you sow does not come to life unless it dies. (15:36).
And what you sow is not the body that will be, but just a seed, perhaps of wheat or something else. (15:37).
But God gives it a body as He has designed, and to each kind of seed He gives its own body. (15:38).
Not all flesh is the same: Men have one kind of flesh, animals have another, birds another, and fish another. (15:39).
There are also heavenly bodies and earthly bodies. But the splendor of the heavenly bodies is of one degree, and the splendor of the earthly bodies is of another. (15:40).
The sun has one degree of splendor, the moon another, and the stars another; and star differs from star in splendor. (15:41).
So will it be with the resurrection of the dead: What is sown is perishable; it is raised imperishable. (15:42).
It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power. (15:43).
It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. If there is a natural body, there is also a spiritual body. (15:44).
So it is written: “The first man Adam became a living being”; the last Adam a life-giving spirit. (15:45).
The spiritual, however, was not first, but the natural, and then the spiritual. (15:46).
The first man was of the dust of the earth, the second man from heaven. (15:47).
As was the earthly man, so also are those who are of the earth; and as is the heavenly man, so also are those who are of heaven. (15:48).
And just as we have borne the likeness of the earthly man, so also shall we bear the likeness of the heavenly man. (15:49).
Now I declare to you, brothers, that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable. (15:50).
Listen, I tell you a mystery: We will not all sleep, but we will all be changed — (15:51).
in an instant, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, the dead will be raised imperishable, and we will be changed. (15:52).
For the perishable must be clothed with the imperishable, and the mortal with immortality. (15:53).
When the perishable has been clothed with the imperishable and the mortal with immortality, then the saying that is written will come to pass: “Death has been swallowed up in victory.” (15:54).
“Where, O Death, is your victory? Where, O Death, is your sting?” (15:55).
The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law. (15:56).
But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ! (15:57).
Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast and immovable. Always excel in the work of the Lord, because you know that your labor in the Lord is not in vain. (15:58).
crossRefs: Isaiah 25:8: He will swallow up death forever.
Hosea 13:14: O death, where are your plagues?
Psalm 110:1: Sit at my right hand until I make enemies your footstool.
Daniel 12:2: Many who sleep in the dust shall awake.

translationNotes.term: Baptized on behalf of the dead
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: טָבַל לַמֵּתִים (ṭābal lamētiym, sense), Greek: βαπτιζόμενοι ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν (baptizόmenoi ὑpὲr tῶn nekrῶn, NT), Aramaic: עמד על מיתיא (עמד על מיתיא)
translationNotes.note: A difficult phrase; denotes a practice in Corinth of baptism concerning the dead; Paul uses it rhetorically without affirming it.

The first portion of each harvest offered to God before the rest could be eaten (Exodus 23:19; Leviticus 23:9-14). Paul calls the resurrected Christ 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep' (1 Corinthians 15:20); the guarantee that the full resurrection harvest will follow.
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בִּכּוּרִים (bikkurim)
Greek: παραδίδωμι (paradidomi) - παραλαμβάνω (paralambano)
translationNotes.note: The pair of verbs in 15:3 is technical. They are the standard terms for handing on a fixed body of teaching word for word, and Paul uses the same pair for the Lord's Supper in 11:23. Jewish teaching used the matching Hebrew verbs, masar and qibbel: the Mishnah opens with Moses receiving Torah at Sinai and handing it on to Joshua, and Joshua to the elders (Avot 1:1). What follows in 15:3-5 is therefore quoted, not composed on the spot.

translationNotes.original: Greek: φθείρουσιν ἤθη χρηστὰ ὁμιλίαι κακαί (phtheirousin ethe chresta homiliai kakai)
translationNotes.note: The line in 15:33 is not Paul's. It is a verse of Greek comedy from Menander's play Thais, in the standard metre of stage dialogue, and it had passed into common speech as a proverb the way lines of Shakespeare have in English. He quotes pagan verse elsewhere too: a line of the poet Aratus in Acts 17:28, and an unnamed Cretan poet in Titus 1:12.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul delivers as of first importance that Christ died for our sins, was buried, was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, and appeared to many witnesses, so denying the resurrection empties the faith; Christ is raised as firstfruits, the dead will be raised imperishable, sown a natural body and raised a spiritual body, and at the last trumpet all will be changed, death swallowed up in victory, so stand steadfast, your labor in the Lord not in vain.

headings.text: Where, O Death, Is Your Victory?

stories.title: 📜 1 Corinthians 16
summaryBullets: Now about the collection for the saints, you are to do as I directed the churches of Galatia: (16:1).
On the first day of every week, each of you should set aside a portion of his income, saving it up, so that when I come no collections will be needed. (16:2).
Then, on my arrival, I will send letters with those you recommend to carry your gift to Jerusalem. (16:3).
And if it is advisable for me to go also, they can travel with me. (16:4).
After I go through Macedonia, however, I will come to you; for I will be going through Macedonia. (16:5).
Perhaps I will stay with you awhile, or even spend the winter, so that you can help me on my journey, wherever I go. (16:6).
For I do not want to see you now only in passing; I hope to spend some time with you, if the Lord permits. (16:7).
But I will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost, (16:8).
because a great door for effective work has opened to me, even though many oppose me. (16:9).
If Timothy comes, see to it that he has nothing to fear while he is with you, for he is doing the work of the Lord, just as I am. (16:10).
No one, then, should treat him with contempt. Send him on his way in peace so that he can return to me, for I am expecting him along with the brothers. (16:11).
Now about our brother Apollos: I strongly urged him to go to you with the brothers. He was not at all inclined to go now, but he will go when he has the opportunity. (16:12).
Be on the alert. Stand firm in the faith. Be men of courage. Be strong. (16:13).
Do everything in love. (16:14).
You know that Stephanas and his household were the first converts in Achaia, and they have devoted themselves to the service of the saints. Now I urge you, brothers, (16:15).
to submit to such as these, and to every fellow worker and laborer. (16:16).
I am glad that Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus have arrived, because they have supplied what was lacking from you. (16:17).
For they refreshed my spirit and yours as well. Show your appreciation, therefore, to such men. (16:18).
The churches in the province of Asia send you greetings. Aquila and Prisca greet you warmly in the Lord, and so does the church that meets at their house. (16:19).
All the brothers here send you greetings. Greet one another with a holy kiss. (16:20).
This greeting is in my own hand — Paul. (16:21).
If anyone does not love the Lord, let him be under a curse. Come, O Lord! (16:22).
The grace of the Lord Jesus be with you. (16:23).
My love be with all of you in Christ Jesus. Amen. (16:24).
crossRefs: Acts 11:29-30: Relief sent to brothers in Judea.
Romans 15:25-26: Paul bringing aid to Jerusalem.
1 Thessalonians 5:6: Be watchful and sober.
2 Corinthians 13:12: Greet one another with a holy kiss.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יוֹם רִאשׁוֹן (ywōm riʾšwōn), Greek: μιᾷ σαββάτου (miᾷ sabbάtou, NT), Aramaic: חד בשבתא (חד בשבתא)
translationNotes.note: Expression used for the day after the Sabbath; refers to Sunday, when believers gathered.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֵרֶם (ḥērem), Greek: ἀνάθεμα (ἀnάthema, NT), Aramaic: חרם (חרם)
translationNotes.note: Term for one devoted to destruction or under ban; here, of anyone who has no love for the Lord.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מָרַנָא תָּא (māranāʾ tāʾ, sense), Greek: Μαρὰν ἀθά (Marὰn ἀthά, NT transliteration), Aramaic: מָרַנָא תָּא (maranā tā)
translationNotes.note: Aramaic phrase 'Maranatha,' meaning 'Our Lord, come!' preserved as a prayer in Greek text.

translationNotes.original: Greek: λογεία (logeia), a collection
translationNotes.note: There was no banking system for moving a fund like this. Coin had to be physically carried by men on foot and by ship, over roads where robbery was common enough that Paul lists it among his hazards at 2 Corinthians 11:26. That is why 16:2 asks each person to set something aside every week rather than scramble at the end, and why 16:3 has the Corinthians choose their own accredited carriers and send them with letters. Romans 15:25-27 and Acts 24:17 record the delivery to Jerusalem.

translationNotes.term: the church that meets in their house
translationNotes.original: Greek: κατ' οἶκον ἐκκλησία (kat oikon ekklesia)
translationNotes.note: There were no church buildings. Congregations met in private houses, and 16:19 names Aquila and Prisca's as one; Romans 16:23 names Gaius as host of the whole Corinthian church. That sets a hard ceiling on numbers, and it also splits the room. A Roman dining room held about nine on its three couches; everyone beyond that ate in the courtyard, where the food and the company were both worse. It is the practical reason the shared meal broke down the way 11:20-22 describes, with one man drunk and another still hungry.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul closes with instructions about the collection, travel plans, commendation of coworkers, greetings, and a final blessing.

intro:
1 Corinthians was written by Paul the apostle (1 Corinthians 1:1), with Sosthenes named as co-greeter in the opening salutation. The letter was composed in Ephesus around AD 55, during Paul's three-year ministry there on his third missionary journey (Acts 19; 1 Corinthians 16:8: "I will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost"). Paul had founded the Corinthian church on his second missionary journey around AD 50-52, an eighteen-month ministry recorded in Acts 18:1-18; he had stayed in the home of Aquila and Priscilla (Jewish-Christian tentmakers who had been expelled from Rome under Claudius's edict against the Jews in AD 49, Acts 18:2), worked alongside them at his tentmaking trade, and preached in the synagogue and in the home of Titius Justus after being expelled from the synagogue (Acts 18:7). The Sosthenes who co-greets the church in 1 Corinthians 1:1 is most likely the same Sosthenes who had been ruler of the Corinthian synagogue at the time of Paul's ministry there and who was beaten by the Greek crowd when Paul was brought before the Roman proconsul Gallio (Acts 18:17); he had evidently become a believer in the years after Paul left. The Corinthian church was beset with problems by the time Paul wrote: members of "Chloe's people" had come to Paul in Ephesus with reports of divisions and immorality in the church (1 Corinthians 1:11), and the Corinthians had also sent Paul a letter asking his guidance on various questions (1 Corinthians 7:1). 1 Corinthians is actually Paul's second letter to the Corinthians; in 1 Corinthians 5:9 he refers to a previous letter ("I wrote to you in my letter not to associate with sexually immoral people") which has not been preserved. Counting that lost letter, Paul wrote at least four letters to Corinth: the lost first letter, our canonical 1 Corinthians, a "severe letter" mentioned in 2 Corinthians 2:3-4 (also lost), and our canonical 2 Corinthians. Paul (originally Saul) was born in Tarsus of Cilicia around AD 5-10 to a Hebrew family of the tribe of Benjamin and was educated in Jerusalem under Gamaliel the Pharisee before his conversion on the Damascus road and his apostolic ministry to the Gentiles; he was martyred by beheading in Rome under Nero around AD 66-67 (see the introduction to Romans for the full biographical sketch).

The historical setting is the wealthy, cosmopolitan, sexually permissive port city of Corinth in the Roman province of Achaia. The original Greek city of Corinth had been destroyed by the Roman general Lucius Mummius in 146 BC; the city had been refounded as a Roman colony by Julius Caesar in 44 BC and rapidly became one of the most important commercial cities of the eastern Mediterranean. Corinth straddled the four-mile-wide Isthmus of Corinth connecting mainland Greece to the Peloponnese, controlling two harbors: Cenchreae on the eastern (Aegean) side and Lechaeum on the western (Adriatic) side. Ships sailing between East and West would often unload their cargoes for porterage across the isthmus on the Diolkos (a paved track) to avoid the dangerous voyage around Cape Malea at the southern tip of the Peloponnese; smaller ships could even be hauled across the isthmus on rollers. This commerce made Corinth wealthy and brought a constant flow of sailors, merchants, travelers, and pilgrims. The city was a Roman colony populated by Italian colonists, freedmen, military veterans, and a substantial Jewish minority. Religion was a marketplace: the temple of Aphrodite atop the Acrocorinth (the city's acropolis) employed temple prostitutes, the temple of Apollo dominated the old forum, and shrines to Isis, Serapis, Asclepius, Demeter, Persephone, and the Roman imperial cult all operated in the city. Corinth's sexual reputation was so notorious that the Greek verb korinthiazomai ("to act like a Corinthian") had become slang meaning "to fornicate." Every two years Corinth hosted the Isthmian Games, one of the four major Panhellenic athletic festivals; Paul's metaphors of athletic competition in 1 Corinthians 9:24-27 ("running the race," "boxing," "exercising self-control like an athlete," "the perishable wreath") would have been immediately vivid to Corinthian readers familiar with the Isthmian Games and the pine-wreath crowns of their victors.

1 Corinthians is the forty-sixth book of the Christian Bible, the seventh book of the New Testament, and the second of Paul's thirteen letters in canonical order. The letter has sixteen chapters. The earliest surviving manuscript is Papyrus 46 (P46, the Chester Beatty II papyrus, c. AD 175-225), which preserves the bulk of the Pauline corpus including 1 Corinthians on a single codex; other early witnesses include Papyrus 11 (P11, 7th century) and the complete copies in Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus (both 4th century AD). Several of the letter's passages have become foundational to Christian doctrine and practice: 1 Corinthians 11:23-26 contains the earliest written record of the words of institution of the Lord's Supper (predating the Gospel accounts by several years); 1 Corinthians 13 is the famous hymn to love ("If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love..."). 1 Corinthians 12-14 also contains the New Testament's most extended teaching on the gift of tongues, which Paul regulates as a phenomenon requiring interpretation for the benefit of the assembly: "If anyone speaks in a tongue, let there be only two or at most three, and each in turn, and let someone interpret. But if there is no one to interpret, let each of them keep silent in church and speak to himself and to God" (1 Corinthians 14:27-28). Paul opens 1 Corinthians 13:1 with "tongues of men and of angels," leaving room for languages beyond ordinary human speech, but his consistent point in chapters 12-14 is that the Greek glossa (whether human or angelic) refers to actual language requiring translation to be intelligible to the hearer, which is why interpretation is necessary in the public assembly. 1 Corinthians 15 contains the earliest creedal summary of the resurrection appearances (15:3-7, which Paul says he had received from those before him) and the New Testament's longest sustained defense of the bodily resurrection.
